  SessionStart total          12,817 bytes
    using-nx-skills SKILL.md   7,507   (routing table / menu)
    session_start_hook.py      5,278   (T2 listing + bead prime)
    nx hook session-start         32
    preflight.py / rdr_hook.py / version_lockstep_hook.py -- 0 bytes when there is
    nothing to report (conditional emitters; they are not the problem)
  SubagentStart total          3,721 bytes

THE DIFFERENTIAL that motivates this:
                     MAIN   SUBAGENT
  plan_search          12        281
  scratch              61        929
  memory_search       149        588
The 3.4x SMALLER channel gets 15-23x the compliance for materially the same
instruction. Suggestive.

CONFOUNDED THREE WAYS -- do not claim causation, and do not let this bead be
described as "the fix":
 (a) PROXIMITY: the subagent directive arrives immediately before its task;
     SessionStart arrives hours before any analytical question exists;
 (b) CONTEXT LENGTH: the subagent's context is short and fresh; by the time the
     orchestrator needs the directive it is far behind;
 (c) COMPETING LAYER: a subagent's prompt carries no "do not call the AgentTool".
Volume is one of four candidate causes. It is simply the cheapest to test.

BUILD -- invert structure, do not just delete text. 7,507 of the 12,817 bytes is a
ROUTING MENU. Menus are reference material and are fetchable on demand; the
imperative is not. So:
 - LEAD with the imperative and its trigger conditions, alone, at the top;
 - move the routing table behind progressive disclosure (the Skill's own body,
   read when the Skill is invoked);
 - keep every trigger CONDITION at SessionStart (the "when"), move every
   destination LIST off it (the "what") -- an agent that knows it should route
   can look up where; an agent that does not know it should route never looks.
 - TARGET: SessionStart under 6,000 bytes, with the imperative in the first 500.

=== VERIFICATION ===
1. BYTE MEASUREMENT, before and after, by the same method that produced 12,817 --
   piping a SessionStart payload through each hook and summing. Assert < 6,000
   and imperative within the first 500 bytes. Mechanical, cheap, non-negotiable.
2. THE REAL TEST, and it must be pre-registered so it can FAIL: after this ships,
   nexus-h33x8.1's census over subsequent sessions must show Skill-invoking share
   of substantial sessions ABOVE the 69.5% baseline, and Serena ABOVE 15.9%.
   Record the prediction in this bead BEFORE landing the change.
3. IF THE NUMBERS DO NOT MOVE, the volume/salience hypothesis is DEAD. Write that
   in the bead and close it as "hypothesis falsified" -- do NOT cut further and
   re-measure. Repeated re-cutting on a dead hypothesis is exactly the
   guidance-layer loop that nexus-4av2n and nexus-3sij7 already document failing
   twice. A negative result here is a genuine deliverable: it eliminates one of
   the four candidate causes and hands the problem to mechanism (nexus-4av2n).
4. NO CONTENT LOSS: every routing destination removed from SessionStart must be
   reachable from the Skill body. Assert by diffing the destination set before
   and after -- otherwise "cut volume" silently becomes "cut capability", which
   would look like success while making the underlying problem worse.

title: census: emit the per-capability census at SessionEnd via the existing nx-session-end-launcher entry (Tier B — live next session, no plugin release)
description:
TIER B (existing hooks.json entry, PyPI-delivered behaviour). Live at the NEXT
SESSION despite the pinned tag. DEPENDS ON nexus-h33x8.1.

WHY TIER B AND NOT A NEW HOOK: hooks.json already has a SessionEnd entry whose
command is `nx-session-end-launcher` (pyproject.toml:132 ->
nexus._session_end_launcher:main). The ENTRY is pinned; the BEHAVIOUR ships in
the wheel. So the census can start emitting at session end WITHOUT touching
hooks.json, WITHOUT a plugin release, and WITHOUT a PENDING_RELEASE.md entry.
Adding a new Stop/SessionEnd entry instead would have been Tier C and dormant for
a full release cycle -- which is precisely the trap conexus/PENDING_RELEASE.md was
written to record (three guards merged, closed as "mechanized", protecting
nothing for the whole window).

BUILD: at session end, emit the per-capability census for THAT session, in the
shape `expectations_census` already uses (ROWS / CLASSIFIED / BLINDSPOT), because
that shape is already read by this project's operators and its BLINDSPOT line is
the single feature that has repeatedly caught false-cleans.

  CAPABILITY  skills=0 nx_answer=0 search=0 serena=0 dispatches=7 bash=150
  BLINDSPOT   <present iff any bucket was unmeasurable>

REPORT COUNTS, NOT VERDICTS. No "you should have used X". The epic's own evidence
(child .6) is that at least one near-zero capability is being correctly declined
on latency grounds. A session-end nag that is wrong even 20% of the time will be
tuned out inside a week, and will take the credible numbers down with it.

KNOWN RISK, state it rather than assume it away: SessionEnd output visibility is
NOT VERIFIED. It is not established that a SessionEnd hook's stdout reaches the
user's transcript (the session is ending). MITIGATION, required, not optional:
ALWAYS write the census to a durable local JSONL (alongside
~/.config/nexus/routing_log.jsonl, the existing precedent) and treat any
on-screen emission as best-effort. The durable log is what makes the trend
queryable later; the screen line is a bonus. If emission proves invisible, the
bead still delivers -- via `nx census capability --since`.
COST: one append per session. No CI job, no runtime cost on the hot path.

=== VERIFICATION ===
1. A session that invoked zero Skills produces a census record containing
   `skills=0`, and that record is FOUND IN THE DURABLE LOG afterwards. The log
   assertion is the real one -- it does not depend on the unverified visibility.
2. VISIBILITY, answered empirically not assumed: run one real session to
   completion and record in the bead whether the line appeared on screen. Write
   down the ANSWER either way. "We did not check" is the failure mode this whole
   epic exists to fix.
3. NON-VACUITY: a session where the transcript is unreadable at end-of-session
   must write a BLINDSPOT record, not a zeroed one. Assert this with a fixture
   that makes the transcript unreadable.
4. NO hooks.json DIFF. `git diff` touching conexus/hooks/hooks.json means the
   change silently became Tier C and is dormant -- if that happens, the bead must
   add a PENDING_RELEASE.md entry and say so, not close quietly. This assertion is
   the one that keeps the tier claim honest.

comments.author: Hellblazer
comments.text:
THE OPEN QUESTION HERE IS ALREADY ANSWERED — BY SOURCE, NOT BY EXPERIMENT (critique
2026-07-31, T2 [21318]). This bead treats "does SessionEnd stdout reach the user?" as
something to settle with a live session. It does not need one, and running the experiment
would produce a null result that is easy to misread as "sometimes visible".

src/nexus/_session_end_launcher.py is explicit in its own module docstring: the launcher
"forks, ``setsid``s, forks again, and redirects stdio to ``/dev/null``". The actual cleanup
runs in a DOUBLY-FORKED GRANDCHILD with fds 0/1/2 pointed at /dev/null, deliberately, so
Claude Code cannot observe it. So a census emitted the natural way — inside
``session_end_flush()`` — is PROVABLY INVISIBLE. Not a coin flip, not
environment-dependent. Verified by reading the file.

THERE IS A VISIBLE PATH, and the same docstring names it: the tier summary "prints AFTER
the fork dispatch", i.e. in the PARENT, post-dispatch. That is where a user-visible census
line would have to go, and it inherits the module's PRE-FORK BUDGET INVARIANT — nothing
slow or network-bound may run before the fork, or it reproduces the "Hook cancelled" race
the module exists to avoid. An offline transcript parse is cheap, but it must be measured
against that budget rather than assumed cheap, and it must sit after the dispatch.

So: drop the live-session experiment, keep the durable JSONL (which was already the
mitigation and is now the PRIMARY artifact, not a fallback), and if a visible line is
wanted, put it on the parent's post-dispatch path with a measured cost. The verification
for this bead should assert WHERE the emission happens, not whether it was seen.

title: [catalog] superseded_by cannot record WHY a collection was retired, and four guards have now tried to infer it — add a retired_reason discriminator
description:
ROOT-CAUSE PROPOSAL after FOUR wrong guards on one column (2026-07-31). Filed under the
standing "root-cause after 3+ patches in the same subsystem" rule. This is a design
proposal, not a defect, and it needs a Hal decision before anyone implements it.

THE PATTERN. Every attempt to gate the rename revive has tried to recover, from
`superseded_by`, information that column does not carry:

  1232585d  liveness  -> a supersede tombstone is non-live AND populated.
  351874c5  identity  -> step 3 and supersedeCollection write the column IDENTICALLY,
                         so it encodes DIRECTION, not PROVENANCE.
  attempt 3 emptiness -> correct, but measures a CONSEQUENCE rather than the fact.

The recorded conclusion was "no predicate over superseded_by can recover provenance; do
not try again." That is right, and the next inference has not been drawn: IF THE COLUMN
CANNOT CARRY THE FACT, STORE THE FACT. Three fixes have gone into inferring something the
schema simply declines to record.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING. `catalog_collections` records THAT a row was retired and WHAT
superseded it. It does not record WHY, and the two why's have opposite safety semantics:

  rename tombstone     children were re-homed FIRST, so the row is empty by construction.
                       Reviving it is the round-trip undo -- the supported operation.
  supersede tombstone  a pure UPDATE, so the row keeps EVERYTHING. Reviving it merges two
                       collections. Never safe, at any emptiness.

Those are different states wearing one representation. Every guard so far has been an
attempt to tell them apart from the outside.

PROPOSAL. Add a discriminator via Liquibase -- `retired_reason TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`
on catalog_collections, written 'rename' by renameCollectionTxn step 3 and 'supersede' by
supersedeCollection. The revive gate then reads directly instead of inferring.

IT DOES NOT REPLACE THE EMPTINESS CHECK, and proposing it as a replacement would repeat
the whole mistake. retired_reason is a claim about how the row GOT here; emptiness is a
measurement of what is there NOW. They fail independently: a bug in step 2 leaves a
'rename' tombstone populated, and emptiness catches what the discriminator would wave
through. Keep both -- the discriminator makes the audit half exact, emptiness stays the
data-safety half.

WHAT IT WOULD HAVE BOUGHT. Attempts 1 and 2 both shipped because the arrangement that
breaks them (supersede X->Y, then rename Y->X) is indistinguishable from a legitimate undo
through `superseded_by` alone. With retired_reason it is a one-column read, and neither
attempt could have been written.

COSTS, honestly: a migration with a backfill question (existing tombstones have no
recorded reason -- '' meaning unknown, and unknown must be treated as UNSAFE, i.e. refuse
the revive, which will annoy anyone mid-undo across the upgrade); one more write on two
paths that must never disagree; and a fifth sense added to a column set the T2 note
already calls overloaded (see [21303], the five tombstone senses). That last one is the
real argument AGAINST: this may be adding vocabulary to a representation that needs
consolidating instead.

I judge it worth doing anyway, because the alternative is a fifth predicate over a column
that has now failed to answer the question four times.

title: [catalog] rename does not touch migration_jobs' JSONB collection set, so an active job can reference a renamed-away collection and its idempotency key silently diverges
description:
Found by the nexus-20890 schema-parity gate on its first real run (2026-07-31). Not a
regression -- a gap the mechanism SURFACED, which is the gate doing its job on day one.

nexus.migration_jobs holds THREE collection-bearing columns that a rename does not touch:

  collections            JSONB  -- the job's whole input SET of collection names
  collections_key        TEXT   -- idempotency key DERIVED from that set (nexus-melvx:
                                   at most one ACTIVE job per (tenant, collection-set))
  per_collection_counts  JSONB  -- progress counters, keyed BY collection name

COLLECTION_SCOPED_TABLES drives a scalar `UPDATE t SET col = new WHERE col = old`. That
statement shape cannot rewrite a name INSIDE a JSONB array or a JSONB object key, and it
must not rewrite collections_key at all -- that value is derived, and forging it would
collide with, or impersonate, a different job's identity under the partial unique index.

So these are correctly EXCLUDED from that list (documented in the gate's
_DOCUMENTED_EXCLUSIONS), but exclusion is not the same as "no problem":

CONSEQUENCE. Rename a collection while a migration job referencing it is QUEUED or
RUNNING, and the job's `collections` array still names the old collection. The job then
resolves a name that no longer exists. Whether that surfaces as a loud failure, a
silently-skipped leg, or a partial migration is UNKNOWN -- I did not trace the job
runner's name-resolution path, and the severity here is provisional until someone does.
Do not treat P2 as established.

The idempotency interaction is the sharper edge: because collections_key is derived from
the ORIGINAL set, a resubmission after the rename hashes to a DIFFERENT key and is not
recognised as the same job. The partial unique index that is supposed to prevent a
duplicate active job would not fire.

OPTIONS, none obviously right:
 (a) refuse a rename while an ACTIVE job references the collection -- fail loud, cheap,
     consistent with the merge-refusal stance the rest of this arc landed on;
 (b) re-home the JSONB references (jsonb_set / array rewrite) and RE-DERIVE
     collections_key in the same transaction;
 (c) accept it and document, if active-job-during-rename is judged not worth defending.

(a) is the smallest correct-by-default move and matches how renameCollectionTxn already
treats hazards it cannot safely resolve. Needs a decision, plus a test either way.

title: engine: topics ON CONFLICT arbiters split across two caller-determined unique keys — id-arbitrated import sites 23505 on idx_topics_root_tenant_collection_label
description:
FOURTH instance of the nexus-0ehwe ON CONFLICT arbiter class, found 2026-07-31 by
extending that bead's audit BEYOND CatalogRepository to every unique key in the
changelog cross-walked against every `onConflict` site in `service/src/main/java`.

## The rule, stated correctly

nexus-0ehwe's audit stated the rule as "an arbiter must be chosen against the table's
COMPLETE unique-key set". That is right but under-specified, and the under-specification
is why it cleared `catalog_links`. The precise rule is:

  An ON CONFLICT arbiter names ONE unique key. Every OTHER unique key on that table
  whose values are CALLER-determined is an unhandled 23505 path. A key whose values are
  SERVER-generated (a BIGSERIAL surrogate) is EXEMPT, because it cannot collide.

`catalog_links` is genuinely clean, but NOT for the reason the audit gave ("arbiters use
the 4-col unique", implying that is its only unique key). It has TWO: `catalog_links_pk
(tenant_id, id)` and `catalog_links_unique`. It is clean because `id` is BIGSERIAL and no
insert site supplies it. Same reason clears `memory` (`id BIGSERIAL`) and the four
`*_etl_dedup` telemetry tables.

## The instance

`nexus.topics` has TWO CALLER-determined unique keys:

  1. `topics_pk` PRIMARY KEY (id)                              taxonomy-001-baseline.xml:58
     — id IS caller-supplied: `TaxonomyRepository:962` and `:1162` both insert TOPICS.ID
       explicitly and arbitrate on it.
  2. `idx_topics_root_tenant_collection_label`
     UNIQUE (tenant_id, collection, label) WHERE parent_id IS NULL
                                                          taxonomy-004-dedup-root-topics.xml:87

And, exactly like `catalog_documents`, DIFFERENT SITES ARBITRATE DIFFERENT KEYS:

  - `TaxonomyRepository:962` (doImportTopic) and `:1162` (batch import) arbitrate
    `TOPICS.ID` only -> exposed to the root-label index. An ETL import of a ROOT topic
    whose (tenant, collection, label) already exists under a DIFFERENT id raises a raw
    23505 that no arm catches.
  - `TaxonomyRepository:1835` and `:1942` arbitrate
    `(TENANT_ID, COLLECTION, LABEL)` WITH `.where(TOPICS.PARENT_ID.isNull())` restated
    -> exposed to the PK instead.

## Corroborating detail worth keeping

Site :1835 restating the partial index's predicate is INDEPENDENT confirmation of a PG
fact verified for nexus-0ehwe against PG 17: a partial unique index cannot be inferred
from its column list alone (SQLSTATE 42P10), and cannot be named via
`ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT` at all, because it is an INDEX and not a CONSTRAINT. So the
codebase already knows how to arbitrate this index correctly in ONE place and not in the
other two.

## Severity

ETL / taxonomy-import path, not the hot read path. Presents as an opaque 500/409 on
`POST /v1/taxonomy/import` for a snapshot whose root-topic ids were reallocated. Lower
than z3ssg (which sits on owner-ensure) but the same defect and the same fix shape:
resolve the non-arbitrated key BEFORE the write.

## Suggested fix

Mirror what landed for the catalog tables: a `resolve-then-write` guard plus the
`UniqueRaceRetry` belt, using the shared `dev.nexus.service.db.SqlConstraints` extractor.
Decide ONE meaning of "this topic already exists" for `topics` and apply it at all four
sites. NOT started.

title: [catalog] collectionIsEmpty counts audit rows as data, so a search or GC pass can falsely block a legitimate undo rename
description:
Found while adding nexus.gc_audit to COLLECTION_SCOPED_TABLES (nexus-v6za0 attempt-3
stacked review, 2026-07-31). PRE-EXISTING property, not introduced by that fix -- filed
because it was noticed, not because the fix caused it.

collectionIsEmpty treats an AUDIT row as data. Four audit tables are in the shared list:
relevance_log, search_telemetry, hook_failures, and now gc_audit. None of them holds
content; all of them are written as a SIDE EFFECT of ordinary reads and maintenance.

The false-positive path: rename X->Y leaves X as an EMPTY tombstone, which is exactly
the state a legitimate undo rename Y->X requires. Then anything that writes an audit row
naming X -- a search that logs telemetry, a GC pass that logs to gc_audit, a hook failure
-- makes X read NON-EMPTY. The undo is then refused with "it still holds data, so
renaming onto it would merge two collections. Purge or restore it first." That message is
FALSE: there is no data and no merge hazard, only an audit breadcrumb. The operator is
told to purge a collection that is already empty.

Severity is deliberately P2 and the direction matters: this fails CLOSED. A false refusal
is loud and recoverable; the failure this whole arc exists to prevent is a false PERMIT,
which is silent and corrupting. Under the standing "no silent fallbacks for
data-correctness problems" directive, over-refusing is the correct side to err on, so
this is a usability defect rather than a safety one.

Options: (a) leave it, document the message as possibly-audit-only; (b) split the shared
list so the emptiness half consults only DATA tables (interacts with nexus-4nll0, which
argues the same split for a different reason); (c) keep audit tables in the emptiness
check but make the refusal message NAME which table held the row, so the operator can see
it is an audit breadcrumb and not content. (c) is cheap, keeps the invariant intact, and
converts a misleading refusal into an actionable one.

Note the interaction: nexus-4nll0 and this bead both push toward splitting the list. If
that split happens, do it ONCE, for both reasons, with the difference enumerated and
tested -- not twice.

title: [bug] the rename merge-guard is under-protected: no index on catalog_document_chunks.collection (now probed 17x2 per rename), zero Python/required-check coverage, and rename_collection_cascade drops the 409
description:
Three residuals from the nexus-v6za0 attempt-3 review round, 2026-07-31. Grouped because
they are all "the guard is right but under-protected", not separate defects.

## 1. catalog_document_chunks has NO index on `collection` — and the probe count just went 5 -> 17

collectionIsEmpty now probes every table in COLLECTION_SCOPED_TABLES, and it runs TWICE per
rename (handler pre-check + txn assertion). Reviewer's measurement:
  - chunks_384/768/1024: PK (tenant_id, collection, chash) -> index-only. Fine.
  - catalog_documents: idx_catalog_documents_collection. Fine.
  - catalog_document_chunks: NO index on collection. PK is (tenant_id, doc_id, position);
    indexes are on chash and doc_id only. -> SEQ SCAN on the largest catalog table, and
    `exists` cannot short-circuit in the EMPTY case, which is the COMMON allowed case.

Bounded (rename verb only, not a hot path), but the widening to 17 tables makes it worth
measuring rather than assuming. ALSO: perf-001-rename-collection-indexes.xml claims "the
other rename/delete-touched tables already have a usable (tenant_id, collection[, ...])
leading index or PK" — the reviewer verified that claim is INACCURATE for this table. A
false statement in a perf changeset is how the next person skips the check.

## 2. No Python / required-check coverage of the merge guard, at all

Zero hits under tests/ and src/ for "merge two collections", "still holds data", "is retired
(superseded". No Python test asserts on any of these 409 bodies.

Layer map: a real request traverses collection_rename.py -> HttpCatalogClient -> HTTP ->
CatalogHandler -> CatalogRepository -> PG. CatalogHandlerRenameTest enters at HTTP (4 of 5
layers, real testcontainer PG — good). CatalogRenameCollectionTest enters at the repo, so
every handler guard is invisible to it. NOTHING enters at the Python client layer.

Combined with nexus-hq9na (service-ci is not a required check on develop OR main), a guard
that has now been WRONG TWICE in shipped code is pinned exclusively by advisory tests. One
integration-marked Python pin driving HttpCatalogClient.rename_collection_cascade against a
live engine would fix it — but note it then compounds nexus-5opzu (integration-only pins go
stale unseen), so it needs a scheduled runner, not just the marker.

## 3. HttpCatalogClient.rename_collection_cascade does not translate 409/500

http_catalog_client.py:~2074. Its sibling supersede_collection, ten lines above in the same
file, maps 404/409 to a legible ValueError. rename_collection_cascade does not, so the new
409s reach the CLI as a raw httpx error. Asymmetry within one file.

title: [bug] cross_model rename from a RETIRED source repoints documents+manifest while chunks stay behind — the x6kdz silent-empty-join strand, permitted by the v6za0 attempt-3 scoping
description:
Found by the code-review of the nexus-v6za0 attempt-3 fix, 2026-07-31. Needs a DECISION,
not just a patch.

That fix scoped handleCollectionRename's source-liveness guard to `!crossModel`, on the
reasoning that the RDR-162 COPY branch never runs step 1, never inserts a registry row and
never touches superseded_by — so a retired SOURCE is harmless there. The reviewer verified
that claim is TRUE as written, and that the scoping does not reintroduce the born-dead
target hole (nexus-c29vr).

BUT "genuinely harmless" is over-broad, and the comment says it. It is harmless for the
BORN-DEAD hazard only. A supersede tombstone is POPULATED. So
`cross_model rename(retired X -> live Y)` is now PERMITTED, and it repoints X's documents
AND its manifest rows to Y while X's chunks_* rows STAY AT X.

That is the manifest-points-at-Y / chunks-live-at-X strand — the silent-empty-join class
of nexus-x6kdz, which rename was already the "second door" back into once.

It is safe ONLY under the RDR-162 premise that Y is a re-embed of X carrying the same
chashes. NOTHING CHECKS THAT PREMISE.

Mitigating, and it lowers the urgency: the reviewer also established that the cost of NOT
widening is milder than the fix's comment implies — remap_collection_references's catalog
cascade is already fail-open (collection_rename.py warns and points at `nx catalog
rebuild`), so a 409 there WARNS rather than failing the migration. The comment's
justification overstated the consequence of refusing.

THE DECISION: either
  (a) narrow the scoping — require the source to be live for cross_model too, accepting the
      warn-and-continue on the migration path; or
  (b) keep it and add a same-chash precondition; or
  (c) keep it and PIN the accepted risk explicitly, so the strand is a recorded decision
      rather than an emergent property.

ALSO OWED regardless: the widened path has NO test.
post_crossModelTrue_ontoExistingTarget_returns200Repoint uses a LIVE source and does not
assert catalog_document_chunks at all.

comments.author: Hellblazer
comments.text:
ADJUDICATION (2026-07-31 stacked review of the v6za0 attempt-3 fix). A reviewer raised the
!crossModel scoping as a CRITICAL, claiming it strands chunks and reproduces the
nexus-x6kdz silently-empty-join class via the SOURCE. I checked it and I do NOT agree.
Recording the reasoning rather than silently overriding the finding.

THE CLAIM: permitting a cross_model rename off a RETIRED source repoints
catalog_documents + catalog_document_chunks to the target while chunks_384/768/1024 stay
behind under the retired name -> stranded chunks, empty join.

WHY IT DOES NOT HOLD: it conflates "the source's chunks remain" with "the join is
broken". They are different things here.
  - Cross-model re-embed PRESERVES CHUNK TEXT, therefore preserves chashes. The COPY
    branch's own comment (CatalogRepository.java, the nexus-x6kdz note) states this: the
    target's chunk rows carry the SAME chashes, so repointing the manifest keeps the
    combined-query join live under the new name. The join resolves against the target,
    which the ETL populated.
  - The source's chunks_<dim> rows staying put is RDR-155 RF-5 BY DESIGN: the source is
    never mutated so a failed migrate is re-runnable from it. That is rollback retention,
    not stranding.
  - x6kdz was the case where documents pointed at the target and MANIFESTS at the source.
    This branch re-homes both. That is precisely the x6kdz fix, not a reintroduction.

WHY THE SCOPING IS A REAL FIX, not a rationalization. remap_collection_references
(src/nexus/collection_rename.py:239) calls catalog.rename_collection(source, target,
cross_model=True) UNCONDITIONALLY, and its catalog cascade is FAIL-OPEN -- it warns and
continues. So with the guard unscoped (HEAD 351874c5 behaviour), a retired source makes
the engine 409, the Python side swallows it as a warning, and catalog_documents is left
pointing at the DEAD source. That is a live data-correctness hole, and the scoping closes
it.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING. The scoping is a NEW permission relative to 351874c5 and it ships
with ZERO test coverage -- no test in CatalogHandlerRenameTest exercises the retired-source
guard in either direction. The residual risk is the caller violating the documented
ordering invariant ("invoke only AFTER the target leg verifies populated"): nothing in the
engine verifies the target is actually populated before repointing. That is true for a LIVE
source too, so the scoping does not introduce it -- but a retired source is a stronger hint
that a migration was abandoned midway, which is exactly when the ordering invariant is most
likely to have been broken.

STILL A HAL DECISION, narrowed to one question: should the cross_model branch verify the
target is populated before repointing, instead of trusting the caller's ordering
invariant? If yes, that is the real fix and it subsumes this bead. Coverage for the
newly-permitted path should land either way.

title: [bug] qc4p1 hook residuals: lock-timeout can write duplicate EXPECT rows (silently inflating N-of-type credit), dedup skipped on empty tool_use_id, no stale-lock reaping
description:
Residuals from the code review of the nexus-qc4p1 implementation (commits f56eb50d,
d970890f, e9788990, in a worktree — NOT yet merged). No Critical or High; the fail-open
discipline, the 0x1f delimiter fix and the ':' charset widening were all verified sound and
mutation-tested. These three are the follow-ups the reviewer raised. Filed here rather than
left in the review, per the standing no-findings-in-prose rule; the reviewer agent belonged
to the worktree session and was not reachable to file them itself.

## 1. MEDIUM — the lock-timeout fallback can write DUPLICATE EXPECT rows

conexus/hooks/scripts/agent-dispatch-expect.sh, the mkdir-lock loop (~118-138).

The loop is bounded at 1s (10 x 0.1s) and `_expect_if_absent` is then called
UNCONDITIONALLY, whether or not the lock was actually held — fail-open by design, so a
dispatch is never delayed indefinitely. But the header explicitly designs for DUAL
registration (plugin hooks.json + project settings.json). If both firings exceed the 1s
budget, both can pass the "not found" check before either writes, producing TWO EXPECT rows
for one tool_use_id.

That directly violates the header's own claim ("two firings must compose to ONE row, or the
N-of-type deficit count is inflated into nonsense"), under precisely the race the lock
exists for. Consequence is worse than a miscount: N-of-type credit is a shared pool, so a
doubled row silently absorbs a genuinely UNDECLARED dispatch of the same type as declared.
That is fail-open-and-silently-WRONG, which is the opposite of the fail-open-and-visible
posture the rest of the hook keeps.

A full fix may genuinely conflict with "never block a dispatch". At minimum the header's
"Idempotent per tool_use_id" claim must be qualified — it currently overclaims.

TEST GAP, same item: TestIdempotence::test_double_registration_writes_one_row
(tests/hooks/test_agent_dispatch_expect.py:277) runs the two invocations SEQUENTIALLY. That
proves the presence-check works; it does not exercise the lock. A genuine pin needs two
subprocess.Popen started without waiting, then joined.

## 2. LOW/MEDIUM — the idempotence guard is skipped entirely when tool_use_id is empty

Same file, `_expect_if_absent`: the guard is
`[[ -n "$DISPATCH_ID" && -r "$FILE" ]] && awk ...`. With an empty DISPATCH_ID the whole
condition short-circuits false and the function calls `expectations_expect`
unconditionally, every firing, with NO dedup.

Measured payloads always carry tool_use_id, so this is probably unreachable — but it is
untested (no payload-without-tool_use_id case under dual firing) and the code has zero
defence if the assumption breaks. The assumption is load-bearing and should at least be
stated where it is relied on.

## 3. LOW — no stale-lock reaping

`expectations_sweep` (tests/e2e/lib/expectations.sh ~523) reaps `*.expectations` older than
7 days and never touches `*.expect.lock` directories. A hook killed between mkdir and rmdir
(OOM, for instance) leaves a permanent stale lock dir, imposing the full 1s retry on every
subsequent Agent dispatch for that session. Bounded and fail-open, so not a correctness
bug — an unbounded-until-session-ends perf tax with no cleanup path. Either steal a lock
older than ~5s, or have the sweep glob `*.expect.lock` too.

## NOT a bead, but record it somewhere durable (item 5 of the review)

N-of-type credit is a shared pool per subagent_type across every EXPECT row of that type,
regardless of provenance. Two dispatches of the same type can borrow each other's
declaration credit. This is INHERENT to the design (no per-instance key exists — the Agent
tool has no name parameter, which is nexus-nu7fo) and not introduced by this diff. But
"declared" therefore means "the type-level count balances", NOT "this specific dispatch was
declared". Someone auditing an individual dispatch will be surprised. Belongs in the
SKILL.md contract or the script header.

title: [bug] service-ci.yml claims its job name is referenced by branch protection — it is not required on develop OR main, so every Java-only pin is advisory at merge
description:
Found while scoping nexus-mijr4, 2026-07-31. VERIFIED against the GitHub API, not
inferred from the workflow file.

.github/workflows/service-ci.yml:101-103 says:

    # NOTE: the job id/display name still say "drift guard" — they are kept
    # verbatim because the PR status-check name is referenced by branch
    # protection; renaming would strand required checks.

That is FALSE. Measured:

  gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/develop/protection --jq .required_status_checks.contexts
    ["pytest (Python 3.12)",
     "CA-3 live (PG from source + pgvector, linux-amd64)",
     "CA-3 live (PG from source + pgvector, linux-arm64)",
     "CA-3 live (PG from source + pgvector, mac-arm64)",
     "engine-service native build (PR trip-wire)"]

  gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection --jq .required_status_checks.contexts
    ["pytest (Python 3.12)", "pytest (Python 3.13)"]

`service-ci` appears in NEITHER. Nothing depends on the name it is protecting.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE STALE COMMENT. The comment reads as reassurance that the
Java suite gates merges. It does not — AGENTS.md line ~119 already states the Java CI is
advisory and does not block auto-merge, but the workflow comment says the opposite to
anyone reading the workflow instead of AGENTS.md.

The practical consequence, which is the real finding: ANY engine invariant pinned ONLY
in a Java test is advisory at merge time. A Python-side lint or contract test rides
`pytest (Python 3.12)`, which is required on BOTH develop and main. This is load-bearing
for where mechanized engine gates should live — it is why the nexus-mijr4 design memo
recommends expressing the liveness-predicate lint in the Python suite (parsing the Java
source) rather than as a Java test.

FIX: either make service-ci a required check, or correct the comment to say what is
actually true. Do not leave a comment that manufactures false confidence about a gate.

ADJACENT (distinct): nexus-5opzu — gates that do not run where people believe they run.

title: [bug] rename_collection_cmd guards the target on T3 chunk presence when correctness turns on the registry's superseded_by
description:
Found by the nexus-5577r terminology census, 2026-07-31.

rename_collection_cmd (src/nexus/commands/catalog_cmds/collections.py:270-306) guards
its SOURCE on the catalog-registry concept and its TARGET on the T3 trashed-document
concept:

  source:  old_row.get("superseded_by")            -> registry.  CORRECT.
  target:  probe_collection_state(t3_db, new)      -> T3 chunks.  WRONG CONCEPT.

The target is exactly where nexus-v6za0 (the silent two-collection merge) happened.

WHY THE CURRENT BEHAVIOUR IS SAFE ONLY BY ACCIDENT:
- A SUPERSEDE-provenance tombstone at `new` still holds all its chunks, so the T3
  probe reads PRESENT and the CLI refuses with "new name already exists in T3". Safe —
  but it refuses because of CHUNKS, not because of the supersession, and the message
  names the wrong reason.
- An EMPTY rename tombstone at `new` — the legitimate round-trip undo — reads ABSENT,
  so the CLI permits it and the engine's identity check decides. So the ONE case the
  CLI's target guard is actually authoritative for is the one it gets right by luck.

A CONCRETE GAP THE ASYMMETRY OPENS: a registry row that is LIVE but CHUNK-LESS
(registered via register_collection before any chunk write — the collection_gc
"junkyard" pattern) reads ABSENT under the T3 probe. The CLI approves; the engine 409s
with "target collection already exists". Fail-closed, but the pre-flight's whole
purpose — gating before side effects — is defeated, and the operator gets the error
from the wrong layer with the wrong explanation.

FIX: read the target's superseded_by. The function already holds a catalog handle
(`cat`) and already does exactly this for the source 30 lines above. Keep the T3 probe
if it earns its place, but the registry check is the one the operation's correctness
turns on.

RELATED, same root, different pair: nexus-mijr4 (the engine's own two liveness readers
are held in agreement by nothing but a comment).

title: 'change one, change both' is a comment: no structural device pins liveCollectionExists against renameCollectionTxn's inlined copy
description:
Found by the re-review of 1232585d, 2026-07-31.

1232585d's central safety property is that the handler's collision guard and
renameCollectionTxn's branch selector never disagree about "is the name taken" again.
The ONLY device shipped to enforce it is a pair of code comments saying "change one,
change both". A comment is not enforcement, and the class already recurred once.

TWO CONCRETE RESIDUALS:

1. The duplication was RELOCATED, not removed. renameCollectionTxn INLINES the predicate
   rather than calling liveCollectionExists, justified as "already inside this txn's ctx".
   That constraint is real but not irreducible: a package-private
   boolean liveCollectionExists(DSLContext ctx, String name), called by both the public
   method (supplying its scoped ctx) and renameCollectionTxn (supplying the transaction's),
   removes the duplication entirely without leaving the txn. That ctx-bound-helper shape is
   already used throughout the file.

2. Nothing pins the AGREEMENT. The mutation check (restore collectionExists in the handler
   -> the round-trip test fails) pins the handler side only. Adding LEGACY_GRANDFATHERED.eq(0)
   to liveCollectionExists and not to the inline copy — a plausible future edit, since
   collectionForTuple carries that filter — reintroduces the class WITH GREEN TESTS.

Project precedent says this is not acceptable as a comment: daemon-lifecycle duplication
lives in a shared primitive with a conformance suite, mechanically enforced by
tests/daemon/test_lifecycle_gate.py. Do the same here.
close_reason: Closed

title: [bug] cross_model:true against an ABSENT target takes the FULL-REHOME branch under a COPY-only flag
description:
Found by the re-review of 1232585d, 2026-07-31.

CatalogHandler.java:1126's new guard fires only when the cross_model target is retired
AND present. With cross_model:true and a target that does not exist AT ALL:
  - guard 1 (collision) is skipped because crossModel is true
  - guard 2 (the new converse guard) is skipped because collectionExists is false
  - renameCollectionTxn finds liveTargetExists == false and runs the canonical
    FULL RE-HOME — moving chunks, taxonomy and aspects

...under a flag whose documented contract is "repoints documents onto an existing LIVE
collection". That is verbatim the sentence 1232585d used to justify adding the guard:
"silently do the more destructive thing under a flag that says otherwise."

The converse mismatch is HALF closed. The commit message claims it closed.

FIX: the guard should key on "target is not LIVE" (absent or retired), not on
"target is retired and present". Both non-live cases want the same 409 under
cross_model, with different remedy text.
close_reason: FIXED on develop 351874c5. The cross_model converse guard now keys on !tgtLive rather than 'retired AND present', so an ABSENT target no longer slips through to the canonical FULL-REHOME branch under a documents-only flag. Error text distinguishes retired from absent. Pin: post_crossModelOntoAnABSENTtarget_409s. Mutation-falsified by reverting to the retired-AND-present form.

title: [bug] handleCollectionSupersede guard 3 accepts a RETIRED superseded_by target, building the chain guard 2 refuses
description:
Found by the re-review of 1232585d, 2026-07-31. Same class as nexus-u4e20 (one
question, two predicates), same handler.

CatalogHandler.java:1043 guards the supersede TARGET with
repo.collectionExists(tenant, supersededBy). Its stated purpose is "or the pointer
dangles and nothing can follow it" — but a RETIRED target is exactly a pointer nothing
can usefully follow. supersede(X -> Y) where Y is already superseded_by = Z constructs
the two-hop unaudited chain that guard 2 refuses from the SOURCE side.

1232585d converted 1 of 4 collectionExists call sites and did not state that the other
three were considered. Full enumeration at the time of that commit:

  CatalogHandler.java:1043  supersede guard 3, on supersededBy   collectionExists   <- this bead
  CatalogHandler.java:1097  rename source guard, on oldName      collectionExists   <- nexus-c29vr
  CatalogHandler.java:1114  collision guard, on newName          liveCollectionExists (converted)
  CatalogHandler.java:1127  cross_model converse                 collectionExists   (deliberate, correct)

Decide whether a retired supersede target should 409, or whether chains through a
tombstone are tolerated by design; either way state it in the code, since the current
silence is what let u4e20 happen.
close_reason: Closed

title: four Docker-backed integration gates errored at setup in one pytest process — mechanism NOT established; 12 same-process cycles clean, original needed ~15
description:
Found 2026-07-31 immediately after reviving these four gates (nexus-ao29z). Filed rather
than left in a commit message.

MEASURED, one observation each way:

  all four files in ONE pytest process:
      uv run pytest tests/db/test_http_combined_query_integration.py \
                    tests/db/test_write_seam_gate_integration.py \
                    tests/db/test_indexer_seam_b_integration.py \
                    tests/db/test_frecency_enehl_integration.py -m integration
    -> 7 passed, 4 ERRORS. All four errors are in test_write_seam_gate_integration.py,
       all at SETUP, all "org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: The connection attempt
       failed."

  each file in its OWN pytest process, sequentially:
    -> 4 passed / 4 passed / 2 passed / 1 passed. All green.

Each file deliberately uses its OWN named pgvector container so the gates "never collide
on a shared Docker container when run concurrently" (test_http_combined_query_integration
docstring). That reasoning covers concurrent SEPARATE processes; it does not cover four
container boot/teardown cycles inside one process, which is what fails.

NOT YET ROOT-CAUSED -- do not implement against this hypothesis. Candidates, in order of
suspicion:
  (a) the documented Docker-Desktop port-forwarding wedge (T2 memory
      project_docker_port_forwarding_wedges: testcontainers stall mid-handshake after many
      container cycles; probe with host psql to the mapped port, expect rc=124). Four
      boot/stop cycles back to back in one process is exactly that shape.
  (b) a fixture teardown that stops a container while a later fixture's pool still holds
      connections against the recycled port.
  (c) genuine resource pressure (four pgvector containers' worth of churn).

Distinguish (a) from (b)/(c) first: re-run the four-in-one-process form and, at the moment
of failure, probe the mapped port from the host with psql. rc=124 means (a) and the fix is
environmental, not code.

IMPACT: low but real. Nobody can run `pytest tests/db -m integration` and trust the
result, which is precisely the invocation someone reaches for after a change to the
service. Given nexus-ao29z left these four unrunnable for three weeks with no signal, the
next person to run them should not meet a second confusing failure mode.

comments.author: Hellblazer
comments.text:
REOPENING — my "REFUTED" closure overclaimed, per critic-arc-0731 (2026-07-31).

The closure ran four CLEAN four-in-one-process runs from a Docker daemon with zero
containers: 12 boot/teardown cycles total. The original failure needed roughly 15 cycles in
one session to appear. So the verification never reached the state the top hypothesis
predicts is required, and — because nothing failed — it never executed the distinguishing
probe this bead's own description prescribed: psql to the mapped port AT THE MOMENT OF
FAILURE, expecting rc=124.

"Not reproduced below the threshold at which it was first seen" is not "refuted". I closed
a P2 on the weaker evidence while the title asserted the stronger claim.

WHAT STANDS: the filed mechanism ("same-process container cycling") is still unsupported —
12 same-process cycles produced nothing. What is NOT established is that the documented
Docker wedge is the cause; that remains the leading hypothesis, untested.

TO ACTUALLY SETTLE IT: drive the daemon past ~15 cycles (loop the four-in-one-process
invocation 4-5 times without clearing containers between), and at the first setup failure
run `psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p <mapped> -U <user> -c 'select 1'` from the host with a timeout.
rc=124 confirms the wedge and this closes as environmental; a clean connect means something
else is going on and the bead is live.

The docstring note in tests/db/test_http_combined_query_integration.py is fine as written —
it already hedges ("suspect ... before the test", "on a healthy daemon") and does not assert
the refutation.

comments.author: Hellblazer
comments.text:
EVIDENCE, 2026-07-31 — one more instance, recorded WITHOUT a closure claim (the last
closure on this bead overclaimed and was reverted; not repeating that).

FULL ENGINE SUITE, single mvn process, ~86 test classes each cycling a
PostgreSQLContainer:

    [ERROR] PgVectorHybridSearchContractTest.startAll:154 » SQL Could not create new connection
            Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 1, Time elapsed: 124.4 s
            Caused by: org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: The connection attempt failed.
            Caused by: java.io.EOFException
    [ERROR] Tests run: 1523, Failures: 0, Errors: 1, Skipped: 1
    GATE-RC=1

Matches the documented signature: failure at CLASS SETUP, EOFException mid-handshake,
~124s elapsed (a timeout, not a refusal), deep into a long single-process run — well
past the ~15-cycle threshold the original instance needed.

DISCRIMINATING EVIDENCE, same tree, immediately after:

    ./mvnw -o test -Dtest=PgVectorHybridSearchContractTest
    Tests run: 17, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Time elapsed: 8.935 s    GATE-RC=0

8.9s standalone vs a 124s timeout in-suite. The class is not broken; the container
handshake is.

WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH:
  DOES  — the failure is not caused by the working-tree changes it ran against (a
          catalog rename/supersede guard change with NO Liquibase changeset, so
          container and schema setup are untouched by the diff), and the class passes
          on that exact tree.
  DOES NOT — establish the MECHANISM. I did not run the host-psql probe the bead
          prescribes, because the container was already torn down when the suite
          ended. To settle it, the probe has to fire AT the failure, which means
          instrumenting the setup path or watching a run interactively.

STILL THE RIGHT NEXT STEP (unchanged from the bead): drive a single process past ~15
container cycles and, at the first setup failure, run host psql to the mapped port with
a timeout. rc=124 confirms the wedge. Until then this is a consistent signature, not a
diagnosis.

title: T2 concurrency latency gate is a ratio of two measured p95s, so it fails on box load, not on regressions (3.22x loaded vs 2.13x quiet, same tree)
description:
Found 2026-07-31 during the nexus-cecqy/g8z8n full-suite gate. Filed rather than left in chat.

test_memory_get_under_concurrent_write_load asserts a RATIO of wall-clock latencies:

    assert load_p95 < baseline_p95 * 3.0

Both terms are measured on the box running the test, so the assertion measures how
loaded that box is, not how the code behaves. MEASURED, same tree, minutes apart:

  loaded box (full 11.5k suite, Docker + leftover testcontainers alive):
    baseline_p95=0.58ms load_p95=1.85ms ratio=3.22x  -> FAILED
  quiet box, file run alone:
    baseline_p95=1.61ms load_p95=3.42ms ratio=2.13x  -> PASSED

Note the direction: it failed with a FASTER baseline. Under load the 0.58ms baseline
sample got lucky, which shrank the denominator and inflated the ratio. A ratio gate whose
denominator is a p95 of a sub-millisecond operation is dominated by scheduler noise; the
tighter the baseline, the more likely a spurious failure. That is backwards from what a
regression gate should do.

Not a correctness defect and not a blocker: the file passes standalone and the run it
failed in was otherwise green (11559 passed). The cost is a false red on local full-suite
runs, which is exactly the signal a pre-push full run exists to give.

RESOLUTION OPTIONS, needs a call:
  (a) Floor the denominator (e.g. max(baseline_p95, 2ms)) so sub-millisecond baselines
      cannot manufacture a ratio. Smallest change, kills the observed failure mode.
  (b) Assert an ABSOLUTE ceiling on load_p95 instead of a ratio -- what an operator
      actually cares about -- with the baseline reported for context only.
  (c) Mark it as a perf test excluded from the routine suite and run it on a quiet gate.

Prior art in this repo: RDR-063's own latency work, and the hybrid-latency single-gate
evaluation (2026-06-17, deferred as nexus-luofb) hit the same class of noisy latency AC.
close_reason:
FIXED on develop, commit b2980b26. Resolution option (a) plus (b) — both, because they
catch different failures.

ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED BY MEASUREMENT, and it is sharper than the bead guessed. Five clean
runs: baseline_p95 1.70-2.18ms, load_p95 1.77-2.08ms, ratio ~1.0x. The FAILING run's
load_p95 was 1.85ms — inside that band. Nothing was slow. Only the baseline was anomalous
(0.58ms, a third of every other observation), and it is the denominator. baseline[94] is
the 6th-slowest of 100 sub-millisecond samples, so it is dominated by scheduler noise, and
the tighter it lands the likelier a spurious failure — backwards for a regression gate.

  (a) The denominator is floored at 1.0ms. That is below every non-anomalous baseline
      observed (1.70ms was the lowest of five clean runs), so the ratio is untouched in
      the regime it is for; the floor only stops a sub-millisecond denominator from
      inventing one.
  (b) A 50ms absolute ceiling on load_p95 — what an operator actually cares about.
      ~24x the highest load_p95 observed and ~11x the highest load_p99 (4.60ms), so it
      cannot fire on noise, and unlike the ratio it cannot be defeated by a lucky
      baseline. Starvation (a read stuck behind a write txn) costs tens to hundreds of ms.

Plus a non-vacuity assert that the sample is not degenerate — a zeroed sample would have
satisfied both.

MUTATION-VERIFIED three ways:
  - +400ms on load_p95           -> ratio fires (227x)
  - baseline 100ms, load 200ms   -> ratio PASSES at 2.0x, ceiling fires (this is the case
                                    (b) exists for; without it the gate is blind on a slow
                                    machine)
  - replay of the reported numbers (0.58 / 1.85) -> passes at 1.85x

The sibling memory_search gate was checked and is NOT affected: it compares load_p50
against a baseline MEDIAN of ~12ms — a robust statistic an order of magnitude above the
noise floor. Left alone deliberately.

title: main's CI still fetches docling models from HuggingFace — the self-hosted-mirror fix is develop-only, so main-targeted PRs keep flaking
description:
Found 2026-07-31. Filed rather than left in chat.

The docling-from-our-own-mirror fix (commit 22a3131b: release asset ci-assets-docling-v1 + NEXUS_DOCLING_ARTIFACTS_PATH + ci.yml repointed) is on DEVELOP. main's ci.yml still pre-fetches docling models anonymously from HuggingFace, with the 3-attempt retry loop whose attempts cost ~25 MINUTES each — a retry budget larger than the job budget, so a genuine HF failure cannot recover and the job is CANCELLED instead.

MEASURED, not theoretical: PR #1433 (a main-targeted PR) had pytest (Python 3.12) burn 30m15s and get cancelled on exactly this — "Data processing error: CAS ..." — while pytest 3.13 passed. It only merged after a manual re-run drew a healthier HF fetch. Any future main-targeted PR is exposed to the same coin flip.

THIS IS THE SAME STRUCTURAL CLASS AS nexus-x7xjj: a fix that lives only on develop does not protect main, and main is where the default-branch behaviour (schedules, and PR-required checks on main-targeted branches) actually runs. x7xjj was the scheduled-workflow half of it; this is the CI-content half.

RESOLUTION OPTIONS, needs a call:
  (a) let the next develop -> main release promotion carry it (zero extra work, but every main-targeted PR until then keeps flipping the coin), or
  (b) a small targeted PR to main with just the ci.yml + pdf_extractor.py change, as was done for the watchdog in PR #1433.

Note the asset itself (ci-assets-docling-v1) is a repo-level release and is ALREADY visible to main's workflows — only the workflow + extractor change is missing there.
close_reason: Fixed on main by PR #1434 (merge fe1a6645, commit f0638816): main's ci.yml now fetches docling models from our release asset ci-assets-docling-v1 via NEXUS_DOCLING_ARTIFACTS_PATH, and the HF cache step carries the explicit 'DOCLING NO LONGER USES THIS' note. Resolution option (b) was taken.

title: [bug] plugin drift ledger cannot see UNCOMMITTED drift — it diffs HEAD against the tag, so it always reports one commit late
description:
Found 2026-07-31 while landing the ERROR_HANDLING.md ttl fix (nexus-cg13x). Filed because I noticed it, said it was "worth a bead", and would otherwise have left it in chat — the exact class Hal called out this session.

tests/test_plugin_release_drift_ledger.py computes drift by diffing the pinned release tag against HEAD. It therefore CANNOT SEE UNCOMMITTED drift, and always reports one commit late.

OBSERVED: the ttl doc fix was edited, gated (full suite green, 11538/0), and committed in a62649ef. The ledger test stayed SILENT through that entire gate and only failed on the NEXT run, after the commit existed. So the author gets told to declare the drift one cycle after the change has already landed on develop — precisely when they have moved on to something else.

WHY IT MATTERS beyond inconvenience: the ledger's own header explains it exists because three guards were once merged, closed as "mechanized", and were protecting nothing, since the installed plugin was still on the pinned tag. A guard that fires one commit late has the same shape as the problem it was built for — it is right, but not at the moment the decision is being made.

FIX SHAPE (not designed): have the drift computation consider the working tree as well as HEAD (git diff <tag> -- <paths> plus unstaged/staged changes), so the ledger fails in the SAME gate as the edit. Care needed: it must not fire on unrelated dirty state, and must stay quiet for files outside the behavioural surface. Alternatively a pre-commit hook, though the suite is the surface that actually blocks.

title: i711w.1 GAP follow-up: engine aggregates + observability pins (merge-candidates/projection-rank/hub-score/audit-histogram endpoints; doctor hook-failure rendering; telemetry/reclaim/consent real-PG semantics)
description:
Follow-up from the nexus-i711w.1 unnumbered GAP triage (candidates 47-49, 56-59 of the final disposition table). title: update_document_collection over-counts: contract says False when already pointed at the target, but the service UPDATE reports 1 affected row on an unchanged value — and the op is missing from CATALOG_WRITE_OPS so it runs through the READER handle
description:
Found during the nexus-i711w C-store port (commit 0c9a0e97), MEASURED by attempting the port
(the ported assertion failed as `assert True is False`), not predicted from a read.

DEFECT 1 — the return value means something different on each substrate.
  Contract (src/nexus/catalog/catalog_writes.py:209-210): return False if the document is not
  found OR is ALREADY pointed at new_collection.
  Client (src/nexus/catalog/http_catalog_client.py:1844-1850): returns `updated > 0`, and the
  service UPDATE reports 1 affected row even when the value is unchanged.
So "already correct" reports True service-side and False locally. Any caller that COUNTS
re-pointed documents — the migrate-fallback-shaped loops — over-counts every document that
was already correct, and reports work it did not do.

DEFECT 2 — the op is missing from CATALOG_WRITE_OPS.
`update_document_collection` is absent from the whitelist in
src/nexus/daemon/catalog_write_shim.py, so it is not recognised as a write and is performed
through the READER handle. Same class as nexus-iltyk (set_alias cross-substrate routing) and
nexus-z0br3 (nx t3 backfill-manifest writing through make_catalog_reader()). Three instances
now, which makes this a pattern rather than three accidents: the write-op whitelist and the
actual set of mutating methods have drifted apart, and nothing asserts they agree.

WORTH DOING WITH THIS FIX: add a tripwire asserting that every method that mutates catalog
state appears in CATALOG_WRITE_OPS. That is the mechanism-level fix; patching the three known
instances leaves the fourth undiscovered. See the standing rule about fixing the shared
primitive rather than one tier's copy.

TEST STATE: the affected test is left PORT-BLOCKED and annotated in
tests/test_catalog_collections.py rather than converted, since converting it would have meant
asserting the buggy behaviour.

title: service-side supersede_collection has NO guards and leaves superseded_at NULL — unknown name silently no-ops, already-superseded is overwritten, new_name may dangle
description:
Found during the nexus-i711w C-store port (commit 0c9a0e97). Source trail verified end to end;
this is what settled the three pinned `pytest.raises(ValueError)` tests in
tests/test_catalog_collections.py.

THE PATH, client to SQL:
  HttpCatalogClient.supersede_collection (http_catalog_client.py:1794-1808) — zero validation,
    just POSTs.
  CatalogHandler.handleCollectionSupersede (service/.../http/CatalogHandler.java:977-988) —
    400s ONLY when `name` or `superseded_by` is absent from the body, which the client always
    sends.
  CatalogRepository.supersedeCollection (service/.../CatalogRepository.java:2292-2303) — a bare
    `UPDATE ... WHERE tenant_id=? AND name=?`, replying 200 {"updated": N} even at N=0.

FOUR MISSING GUARDS that the local implementation had:
  1. old_name not registered -> silently no-ops (updated=0, still 200).
  2. already superseded -> silently overwritten, no conflict signalled.
  3. superseded_by (new_name) not registered -> writes a DANGLING pointer.
  4. superseded_at is left NULL. Local stamps datetime.now(UTC) itself; the client's
     superseded_at param defaults None and is omitted from the payload, the handler passes "",
     and tsOrNull("") -> NULL. So a superseded row cannot be ordered or aged.

There is NO exception type to convert the local tests' assertions to, which is why they stay
pinned rather than ported. They become the regression tests when the guards land.

RELATED AND PROBABLY THE SAME ARC: nexus-cecqy already records that service-mode RENAME
DELETEs the old collection row (renameCollectionTxn step 3, FKs ON UPDATE NO ACTION), after
which supersede_collection updates 0 rows and the CLI still echoes "Emitted
CollectionSuperseded". Guard 1 above is exactly what makes that silent. Fix these together —
the guards are what turn cecqy's silent no-op into a loud failure.

Also note supersede_collection SEMANTICS have no service-side test at all (the only existing
one asserts `result is None`, i.e. wire shape). That is item 14 on nexus-i711w.1 and is a
Stage-2 exit criterion.
close_reason:
FIXED on develop, commit 1d854b7a. All four guards, plus a fifth the bead did not name.

/collections/supersede was a bare UPDATE replying 200 {"updated":0} to every bad input,
and HttpCatalogClient discarded the count, so every one of them was silent. Guarded in
CatalogHandler.handleCollectionSupersede rather than in the repo, matching the sibling
verb handleCollectionRename which already carries its 404 (nexus-hz785) and 409
(nexus-gaou3) that way and keeps the repo method a pure UPDATE.

  guard 1  unregistered old_name            -> 404
  guard 2  already superseded, DIFFERENT     -> 409, original pointer survives
  guard 3  unregistered superseded_by        -> 404, nothing written
  guard 4  superseded_at                     -> stamped now() server-side (DB clock) when
                                                the caller supplies none. No caller ever
                                                did, so every supersession recorded to
                                                date is undatable.
  guard 0  name == superseded_by             -> 400. Not on this bead; a self-referential
           (NEW)                                tombstone is permanently excluded from
                                                collectionForTuple with nothing to
                                                redirect to. Its sibling rename verb
                                                refuses the identical old==new case.

Guard 2 carves out the SAME target deliberately, and that carve-out is pinned by its own
test. Re-asserting an existing supersession is not "chaining a second supersede event" --
it is the ordinary state after a rename, which under nexus-cecqy now tombstones X -> Y
itself and whose caller then issues supersede(X, Y). The same-target path returns
{"updated":1} WITHOUT re-running the UPDATE, so a retry cannot move the recorded instant.

Client: HttpCatalogClient.supersede_collection maps 404/409 onto ValueError carrying the
engine's own explanation (a new _engine_error_detail helper); a 500 still raises
HTTPStatusError, since an outage must not read to callers as "you passed a bad name".

Two call sites needed the refusal handled: migrate-fallback was unguarded and would have
aborted a COMPLETED migration with a traceback (it now reports what did and did not
happen), and the doctor's printed remediation recipe registers the target before
superseding -- an ordering that is now load-bearing and is commented as such.

PINS: tests/db/test_i711w_gap_xfails.py item 14 (4 guard tests, xfails removed) plus a new
same-target idempotence test; service CatalogHandlerRenameTest gains 7 HTTP-level tests
(the route had NO supersede coverage at all); tests/catalog/test_http_catalog_client.py
gains the ValueError-mapping pins including the 500-is-not-a-ValueError case.

Mutation-verified: stripping the guard block and the timestamp default fails exactly the
five expected tests and nothing else.

Engine 1530 tests / 0 failures. Python 11559 passed / 0 failures.

DEPLOY DEPENDENCY: engine-side, so it reaches users via an engine-service tag + conexus
deploy. The client half is safe ahead of it -- against the current engine these statuses
never occur, so nothing raises that did not raise before.

title: nx t3 backfill-manifest writes through a READER handle — reachable, opaque on the SQLite arm, and works only by accident on the service arm
description:
Found during the nexus-i711w C-store port (commit 1f6d0b89), verified in source.

THE PATH. commands/t3.py:115-133 `_make_catalog()` returns `make_catalog_reader()`.
Per factory.py:143-155 that is, on the SQLite arm, "a read-only local Catalog ... opens its
SQLite handle" in mode=ro. The backfill command then hands that handle to a WRITE site:
  commands/t3.py:717   backfill_manifest_for_collection(cat, t3_db, coll_name, ...)
  catalog/manifest_backfill.py:246   catalog.write_manifest(doc_id, chunks)

So `nx t3 backfill-manifest --no-dry-run` on the SQLite arm attempts a write on a mode=ro
handle. The failure is then caught by the blanket `except Exception` at commands/t3.py:727,
echoed as `ERROR in {coll_name}: attempt to write a readonly database`, appended to errors,
and the loop continues. Not silent, but opaque: the operator sees a SQLite errno message for
what is actually a wiring defect, per collection, and the command still exits having
backfilled nothing.

WHY NO TEST CAUGHT IT. Untested by construction. Every test of this path patches
`_make_catalog` with something writable, so the reader/writer mismatch is never exercised.
That is why the C-store port KEPT the patch here (pointing it at ActiveCatalog, which routes
writes through make_catalog_writer) rather than dropping it the way the test_t3_gc port did
at commit 085009fe — dropping it would have failed those tests for a reason unrelated to
their subject.

WHY THIS IS STILL WORTH A BEAD THOUGH THE SQLITE ARM IS BEING DELETED. The concrete
mode=ro breakage does die with the local Catalog in nexus-i711w. What SURVIVES is the design
defect: a write site is being fed a handle obtained from the READER factory. On the service
arm it happens to work — HttpCatalogClient / the shared service handle proxies the write —
so after i711w this reads as correct code while actually relying on the surviving substrate
being permissive about a contract the factory split exists to enforce. The next reader has
no way to see that `cat` here is a reader.

FIX (small, and better done while the two-arm contrast still exists to test against): the
backfill command should obtain a WRITER for the write path — make_catalog_writer(), or the
same daemon write-shim route ActiveCatalog uses — rather than passing the reader handle. If
a reader is genuinely wanted for the dry-run path and a writer only for --no-dry-run, make
that split explicit at the call site.

Do NOT "fix" this by relaxing the reader. The read-only reader is the invariant (RDR-176
Phase 1 Gap 2: in service mode the local .catalog.db is a FROZEN MIGRATION SOURCE that must
not be mutated, enforced by tests/catalog/test_rdr176_catalog_non_mutation.py).

RELATED: the same file's GC verb has two other open holes on the service arm — nexus-jqrtp
(the empty-alive-set abort guard is unrepresentable there) and item 20 on nexus-i711w.1
(ChunkOrphaned audit records are not emitted there at all). Three separate defects on the
same command family, all invisible from the SQLite arm's green tests.

title: manifest_write_batch_hook does not reach its failure path under the SERVICE catalog — port residue from nexus-i711w C-store
description:
Residue from porting tests/test_catalog_manifest_read_api.py off the local

title: [bug] t2_migration_flock can deadlock a single process against itself — LOCK_EX on a second fd for the same lock file
description:
Found while fixing tests during nexus-i711w Stage 2 sub-stage C. Not caused by that work; exposed by it.

THE DEADLOCK. nexus/db/migrations.py t2_migration_flock() opens the lock file and takes a BLOCKING fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX). flock is per-open-file-description, not per-process, so two separate os.open() calls on the same path in ONE process contend with each other. A blocking LOCK_EX therefore waits forever.

The reachable path, observed:
  commands/upgrade.py:630  with t2_migration_flock(db_path.parent): apply_pending(...)
  commands/upgrade.py:708  _run_upgrade constructs T2Database(...)
  db/t2/__init__.py:383    T2Database.__init__ -> bootstrap_schema
  db/t2/__init__.py:708    bootstrap_schema -> t2_migration_flock(path.parent)   <-- blocks

Observed as two pytest runs sitting at 48 and 64 minutes elapsed with ~2 SECONDS of CPU each. Confirmed by PYTHONFAULTHANDLER stack dump: both parked in fcntl.flock at migrations.py:2879. Only reproduced when pending_t2 is empty, which is why it is not hit routinely.

THE DOCSTRING ASSERTS THE OPPOSITE, and that is the part worth fixing first. t2_migration_flock's docstring says: 'Consistent ordering means the daemon-startup and upgrade migration paths cannot deadlock even if ever run concurrently in one process (code-review finding).' Lock ORDERING protects against ABBA deadlock between two different locks. It does nothing about the same lock acquired twice on different fds, which is what happens here. A reader who trusts that sentence will not look for this.

WHY IT IS P2 AND NOT P1: bootstrap_schema early-returns in SERVICE mode (db/t2/__init__.py:655), which is the shipping default in both local and cloud mode, so the second acquisition does not happen on a normal install. It bites =sqlite paths and tests that pin SQLite.

FIX DIRECTIONS (not chosen):
  a) reentrancy guard — a process-local set of held lock paths, skip re-acquiring;
  b) pass the already-held state down so bootstrap_schema does not re-lock;
  c) LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB with an explicit 'already held by this process' branch.
Whichever is picked, correct the docstring: the current sentence is the reason this was hard to see.

Refs nexus-i711w
close_reason: Queue-triage sweep 2026-08-19 (Sam-authorized, 8-agent verify-or-flag fleet, verified against develop @ 33d0c453e): SUPERSEDED. Evidence: t2_migration_flock no longer exists anywhere in src/ or tests/ — the SQLite T2 migration path it deadlocked died with the RDR-158 retirement; nothing left to fix

description:

tests/test_release_artifact_verb_rot.py sweeps .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md, tests/e2e/**/*.sh + service/native-smoke.sh, and .github/workflows/*.yml run: bodies. Sub-stage B's review found dead 'nx daemon t2 ...' invocations in FOUR trees it does not cover:

All were fixed by hand in the sub-stage-B review-fix commit. The tripwire's own docstring frames its charter as 'release-only artifacts' — conexus/ is a shipped artifact and arguably already in charter, so extending to it is closer to a bug fix than new scope. scripts/ is the same rot class as tests/e2e/**.

Cost is near zero (a grep test, no new CI job). Precision risk: scripts/ and conexus/ carry prose that legitimately narrates retired verbs, so the fenced-code / non-comment-line discipline the existing sweep uses would need to carry over, plus the _FILE_VERB_ALLOWLIST escape valve.

title: catalog_write_shim is 90% dead after the T2 daemon retirement, and its surviving tuple lives in daemon/ where it does not belong
description:
FOUND during nexus-i711w Stage 2 sub-stage B, deliberately NOT fixed there to
keep that commit scoped to "the daemon modules are gone".

src/nexus/daemon/catalog_write_shim.py splits cleanly:

SURVIVES — real, load-bearing, and NOT daemon-related:
  CATALOG_WRITE_OPS  (the 23-op write whitelist)
    consumed by src/nexus/catalog/factory.py — BOTH CatalogWriter and
    HttpCatalogWriter enforce it — and referenced by
    src/nexus/catalog/catalog_protocol.py, whose CatalogWriter protocol is
    specified as "method set is exactly CATALOG_WRITE_OPS".

DEAD — zero production consumers once t2_daemon.py / t2_client.py were deleted:
  build_catalog_write_dispatch   (built the daemon RPC dispatch table)
  CATALOG_WRITE_PREFIX           ("catalog_write." RPC namespace)
  make_write_shim                (per-op Tumbler-coercing RPC shim)
  encode_tumbler_args            (wire encode)
  decode_return                  (wire decode)

TWO THINGS TO DO:
 1. Delete the five dead symbols.
 2. MOVE CATALOG_WRITE_OPS out of src/nexus/daemon/. A catalog write whitelist
    consumed only by catalog/ has no business living under daemon/ — and with
    the shim's daemon half gone there is nothing daemon-shaped left in the file.
    Natural home: src/nexus/catalog/ (alongside catalog_protocol.py, which is
    its main semantic partner).

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS — an existing gate is now WRONG:
tests/daemon/test_rdr173_registry_carveout.py declares

    _P4_DELETE_SET = {"t2_daemon", "discovery", "spin_guard",
                      "t1_lease", "t2_client", "catalog_write_shim"}

i.e. it expects catalog_write_shim to be DELETED at P4. It cannot be, because
catalog/factory.py imports from it. The gate passes only because it checks a
narrow question — that the SURVIVING daemon modules (service_registry.py,
aspect_worker_daemon.py) do not import the delete set — and never checks
non-daemon importers. So the declared P4 delete set has been wrong about this
module for a while, invisibly. (Same is true of "t1_lease", which the RDR-149
conformance suite imports.)

The move in (2) is what makes the carve-out honest: once the tuple lives in
catalog/, catalog_write_shim.py really can be deleted as _P4_DELETE_SET says.

RELATED, same session, same class (stale declarations that degrade silently
rather than failing): test_lifecycle_gate.py's _FLOCK_ALLOWED_MODULES and
test_kmo9h_catalog_gate_census.py's _RAW_ALLOWED both carried entries for
daemon/t2_daemon.py; storage_boundary_lint carried "src/nexus/daemon/" in three
allowlists. All four were removed in sub-stage B — an allowlist entry nothing
needs is standing permission for whatever lands there next.

title: RDR-149 conformance still lists 't3' as a tier after P4b retired the T3 daemon — phantom tier or deliberate generic harness?
description:
FOUND during nexus-i711w Stage 2 sub-stage B, while removing "t2" from the same
tuple.

tests/daemon/test_rdr149_lifecycle_conformance.py:68
    TIERS = ("t1", "t2", "t3", "storage_service", "aspect_worker")

"t3" is still there, but the supervised Chroma T3 daemon was retired by
RDR-155 P4b — the Java storage service serves T3 in every mode now. Corroborating
evidence that the tier is dead:

  - tests/daemon/test_discovery.py:77 says the T3 discovery arm is "retired with
    the managed-chroma daemon — only 't2' resolves".
  - src/nexus/commands/upgrade.py's _cycle_supervised_daemons_to_current has a
    comment saying the supervised Chroma T3 daemon is retired; only
    _cycle_storage_service_to_current remains.
  - grep for a t3 daemon tier in src/ finds only `nx t3` (the T3 STORE command
    group in cli.py), which is a different thing.

TWO READINGS, and they want different fixes:

 (a) PHANTOM TIER. P4b removed the T3 daemon but left its row in the conformance
     matrix, so `T3RecordHarness` now proves lease semantics for a tier nothing
     publishes. `test_every_cell_covers_all_tiers` then enforces completeness of

 (b) DELIBERATE. The harnesses are tier-STRING-generic: `_LeaseHarness` with
     `_REGISTRY_TIER = "t3"` exercises ServiceRegistry lease mechanics with
     synthetic pids and never touches a real daemon. On that reading the row is

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: CLAUDE.md makes this suite the mechanical
enforcement point for "daemon-lifecycle fixes land in the shared primitive,
never one tier's copy" (RDR-149, gate = tests/daemon/test_lifecycle_gate.py). If
the matrix can carry dead columns silently, the gate's completeness assertion is
weaker than it reads.

rather than failing. Sub-stage B removes that one. Worth checking whether P4b
left a "daemon/t3_daemon.py" style entry anywhere too.

title: RDR-126 §3 first-run banner has no producer after the T2 daemon retirement — decide its disposition
description:
nexus-i711w Stage 2 sub-stage B deleted `mcp/_first_run.ensure_installed_and_running`
(it installed the T2 daemon's autostart unit and shelled out to
`nx daemon t2 ensure-running`). That function was the SOLE producer of the
RDR-126 §3 first-run banner.

WHAT IS NOW PRODUCER-LESS in src/nexus/mcp/_first_run.py:
  maybe_banner / queue_banner / BannerSpec / _PENDING_BANNER
  apply_first_run_banner_instructions  (still called from mcp/core.py main())
  deliver_pending_banner               (already had NO production caller
                                        before this change — tests only)
  mark_shown / _first_run_marker_path  (marker still read by
                                        installer.uninstall_daemon)

WHY IT WAS NOT DECIDED IN SUB-STAGE B: RDR-126 §3 is a separate numbered
surface with its own test file (tests/test_first_run_banner.py, ~370 lines) and
its own mcp/core.py startup wiring. Folding it into a daemon sub-stage is
exactly the bleed the B/C/A split exists to avoid (deletion-discipline rule 2).
A tombstone comment in _first_run.py records the consequence at the code.

THE DECISION IS NOT "does anyone lose a feature": the banner ALREADY never
fired on a service-backed install, because ensure_installed_and_running
returned early in service mode (RDR-176 Phase 1) before ever queueing one. So
on the post-Stage-2 substrate this is dead code, not a live capability.

OPTIONS:
 (a) DELETE the subsystem + its test file + the core.py call. Cleanest; removes
     text that now describes a nonexistent "background knowledge daemon that
     runs at login".
 (b) RE-POINT it at a surviving first-run event (e.g. `nx init` installing the
     SERVICE autostart unit). This would be NEW capability, not preservation —
     no service-mode first-run banner exists today.

RECOMMEND (a), with (b) filed separately if the Desktop/plugin-first onboarding
story wants a banner. Note nexus-4xgfy calls Desktop/plugin-first the dominant
post-upgrade path, so (b) may be worth its own bead regardless.
